title: Dry seasons
hook: every practitioner meets seasons when practice feels empty
tomorrow: what did the Buddha tell a town full of doubters?

segments.voice: Yesterday, one breath for a child: Rahula's water vessel and mirror, and a kids' class with room for chants and breathing both. Mai's Sundays are going fine. Her own mornings aren't.
screen: `ONE BREATH FOR A CHILD.` → `HER OWN MORNINGS AREN'T.`

segments.voice: Some mornings the cushion feels like a waiting room: you sit, the timer runs, and nothing happens. Mai has had a whole week of those. Meanwhile, out on the patio, her grandfather, Ông Thanh, is watering a bonsai that hasn't put out a new leaf since fall. He presses a thumb into the soil, smells the wet dirt, and waters it anyway. Nothing on top. Something underneath, maybe. The Buddha had a picture for exactly this, and it's a farmer.
screen: `THE CUSHION AS A WAITING ROOM.` → `A BONSAI WITH NO NEW LEAVES.` → `ÔNG WATERS IT ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: In a short sutta of the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha describes a farmer with three urgent jobs: plow the field well, sow the seed in time, let the water in and out. That's the farmer's work. What the farmer can't do, the Buddha says, is command the crop: sprout today, grow ears tomorrow, ripen the day after. The crop comes up when its time comes. Then he turns the picture toward practice. A practitioner also has urgent work: training in conduct, in the mind, in wisdom. And no one has the power to say: let my mind be free today. It ripens in its time. It's a humbling picture, and a kind one. That's the Buddhist answer to a dry season. Not a trick to make the sitting feel full again. Do the farmer's part: sit, keep the precepts, keep coming back, and stop demanding a harvest on a schedule. Some teachers call dry stretches an ordinary part of a long practice, not proof that it's failing. A field in winter looks dead. It's resting. Ông's bonsai is a very small field: a little water, a lot of patience, and roots doing work that nobody sees.
screen: `PLOW, SOW, WATER.` · `NO FARMER COMMANDS THE CROP.` · `THE MIND RIPENS IN ITS TIME.` · `DO THE FARMER'S PART.` · then, large: `KEEP SITTING.`

segments.voice: If there's a plant near you, press a fingertip into its soil and notice it: cool or warm, damp or dry. If not, press your palms flat on the floor. Then sit the way the farmer waits, the work done and nothing demanded. When your mind asks whether anything's happening, let the answer be: roots.
Dry seasons: stretches when practice feels empty. The farmer keeps plowing and watering, and the crop comes in its own time.
Keep sitting: the field is resting, not dead, and the roots are still at work. See you in the morning.

screen: `DAY 1754 COUNTS.` → `A LIFE OF PRACTICE · 29 OF 45.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DID THE BUDDHA TELL A TOWN FULL OF DOUBTERS?`

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often encourage practitioners to keep a steady daily sit through stretches that feel empty, keeping the precepts and returning to the cushion without demanding results.

match.prompt: the farmer's part — tap the pairs.

myth: a dry stretch in practice means you're doing it wrong
in the farmer simile the crop comes in its own time; the work is to keep tending.
in the sutta, a farmer who works harder can make the crop ripen faster
he does his three jobs; the ripening isn't his to command.
the Buddha compares freeing the mind to a crop coming up in its season
it ripens when its time comes, not on demand.

fork.setup: your friend has journaled every night for a month, and lately it feels pointless, just words on a page. what fits the farmer simile?
options: stop for now and wait until the feeling comes back.
keep the small habit going; what's growing may not show yet.
double the time each night until it feels meaningful.
fork.reveal: the farmer plows, sows and waters, and can't order the crop up. keep tending, and stop demanding a harvest on schedule.

original.note: Pali: farmer, plowman. The Buddha's picture for a practitioner who tends the field and waits.

trapdoor: what you thought: if practice feels empty, it isn't working.
what it means: the farmer tends the field, and the crop comes up in its own season.
what a scholar hears: Anguttara Nikaya 3.91, the 'urgent' sutta: three urgent duties for the farmer, and three for the practitioner, higher conduct, mind and wisdom.
guess: stretches when practice feels empty and flat
the hot months when monks travel to teach
the fasting days before a big temple festival

chat.says: a whole week of sitting and NOTHING. like staring at a wall. am i doing it wrong?
options: probably not. the farmer plows and waters, then waits. the crop isn't on your clock.
yes. if nothing's happening, switch methods until something clicks again.
push harder. sit twice as long and you'll break right through the wall.
chat.meaning: In AN 3.91 the farmer can't order the crop up today; it ripens in its season. A dry stretch calls for tending, not a harvest on demand.

tie.story: The Buddha's farmer plows, sows and waters, but can't command the crop to come up today.
tie.friend: Mai can keep sitting through her flat week, the way Ông waters a bonsai with no new leaves.
tie.you: what are you tending this month that hasn't shown anything yet?

Ông Thanh.meaning: Grandpa Thanh, Mai's grandfather, who keeps bonsai

Anguttara Nikaya.meaning: a collection of the Buddha's discourses, grouped by number

sutta.meaning: one of the Buddha's recorded discourses

precepts.meaning: the training rules Buddhists take on, such as not killing or lying

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.91 (Accayika Sutta: the farmer's urgent duties; numbered 3.93 in some editions)

notes: Shape: senses (soil under a fingertip, wet dirt; the practice is touch). Mai's storyline: a flat, dry week of sitting at home; Ông Thanh waters his bonsai anyway (the elder's weekly appearance).

AN 3.91 (Accayika) paraphrased: the farmer's three urgent duties (plow and harrow, plant seed, let water in and out); he has no power to say 'let my crops spring up today, have ears tomorrow, ripen the next day'; likewise the monk's three urgent duties (higher virtue, higher mind, higher discernment) and no power to say 'let my mind be released today'. Numbering differs by edition (3.91 / 3.93); confirm.
'Some teachers call dry stretches an ordinary part of a long practice': general teacher advice, not from the cited sutta. Confirm phrasing.
Surprising fact: the Buddha says even a hard-working farmer can't command a crop to sprout today, and the mind's release is the same (AN 3.91).
